items.title: Harry "Sweets" Edison interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: So he had to go with Fletcher Henderson for the rest of his life.

ctx.x: Yes, because in my era, as you know, there was a lot of prejudice toward the musicians because we couldn’t play in a studio band, they had radio bands that were getting paid weekly, they were on a salary. They had musicians here at Fox Studio, MGM, Metro Goldwyn Mayer, they were all on staff. And they got paid whenever they worked or played. But they didn’t have black musicians at the time. So our only course was to play solos. And when you picked up your horn, you’d get you a “Georgia Brown” or something,…

to do. They could be with their families, you know? But we had to take to the road. And as I was telling Wynton Marsalis, I made a CD with him last week. And I told him that you know there were quite a few good, legitimate trumpet players years ago, but they had no place to play. There was one guy, Russell Smith, he was the greatest student Bach had. He learned the trumpet, oh there was no kind of concert trumpet he couldn’t play. But he couldn’t get a job. So he had to go with Fletcher Henderson for the rest of…
Yes. We were just talking about that section that he was in.

items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Russell Smith, he had all that learning, he ended up playing with Fletcher Henderson all his life.

ctx.x: Well, this has been years ago…Tchaikovsky? One of the great directors. But he ended up playing first in that. The time was just right for Wynton to do that. There was a color barrier when we came up, what was the use of …. Russell Smith, he had all that learning, he ended up playing with Fletcher Henderson all his life. And I played with Count Basie, I never had no learning. There’s Wendell Culley ended up all his life playing with Count Basie and Noble Sissle.
It’s not that the talent or the ability wasn’t there, it was the opportunity.

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: Fletcher had a good band and he always wrote in the hard keys.

ctx.x: No, I meant about the reading and everything? You could --

Yeah. Yeah, yeah, but it still wasn't -- you know, it took a lot of rehearsals to get what you wanted to get. And they had one guy, Chappie Willett, he used to write such hard arrangements it would take so long to get these players together. And musicians could read in those days, because Don Redman had a fantastic band. So did Duke. So did Jimmy Lunceford. So did Fletcher, Fletcher had a good band and he always wrote in the hard keys. That's why all the good musicians came out of Fletcher's band, you know.

In fact, all the musicians in those days were good musicians. They knew how to read. [But Basie's band was based on head arrangements because everybody took solos in Basie's band. Basie's band wasn't an ensemble band. It was noted for soloists, you know. Everybody was a fantastic soloist.]
